comparison: Perfect agreement on sleep phenotype findings (C3, C38-C46). Both evaluations find the data well-supported. OpenEval notes appropriate caution about sample size (n=6), while peer reviewers describe the experimental design as 'robust' with 'solid experimental data.'

Perfect agreement on circadian rhythm findings (C4, C47-C57). Both evaluations support these claims. OpenEval highlights the importance of normal tau but impaired rhythm quality, while peer reviewers describe the data as 'sound' and note the comprehensive investigation of circadian disturbances.

Perfect agreement on light response deficits (C5, C58-C62). Both evaluations find these behavioral findings well-supported by multiple independent assays. OpenEval notes appropriate presentation of mechanistic inferences as suggestions, while peer reviewers accept these as part of comprehensive characterization.

Strong agreement on anatomical and functional findings linking retina to SCN (C6, C63-C66). Both evaluations support these claims. OpenEval notes mechanistic links are appropriately speculative, while peer reviewers treat these as part of robust experimental design without concerns.

Perfect agreement on mechanistic interpretation of intact core clock with input/output deficits (C68-C73). Both evaluations support these claims. OpenEval notes speculative mechanisms are appropriately presented, while peer reviewers accept this as sound interpretation providing thorough understanding.

Partial overlap on behavioral phenotypes (C8-C9). Both evaluations support baseline behavioral deficits. OpenEval focuses on validation of multiple behavioral assays, while peer reviewers emphasize the relationship between behavioral deficits and sleep patterns in the context of TRF intervention.

Strong agreement on correlations between sleep and behavior (C10, C76-C79). Both evaluations support these correlational findings. OpenEval appropriately notes correlation does not establish causation, while peer reviewers accept these correlations as part of comprehensive investigation linking sleep to behavioral outcomes.

Strong agreement on TRF improvements in circadian rhythm and sleep (C11-C12, C82-C83, C119-C127). Both evaluations find these intervention effects well-supported. OpenEval highlights specificity to rhythm quality, while peer reviewers explicitly state TRF 'improved sleep, circadian, and social behaviors.'

Strong agreement on TRF improvements in sleep parameters (C12, C84, C123-C127). Both evaluations support these findings. OpenEval notes sleep improvements parallel circadian improvements, while peer reviewers confirm TRF led to 'improved behavior' and 'enhanced cognitive/behavioral capacities.'

Strong agreement on TRF behavioral improvements (C13, C85-C87, C128-C133). Both evaluations find these claims well-supported. OpenEval emphasizes statistical significance and specificity, while peer reviewers explicitly confirm 'scheduled feeding...improved sleep, circadian, and social behaviors.'

Strong agreement on TRF as proof-of-principle intervention (C14, C88). Both evaluations support translational potential. OpenEval notes appropriate speculation about mechanisms, while peer reviewers endorse 'potential therapeutic avenues' and state findings 'may offer new insights into...potential treatment strategies.'

Perfect agreement on cytokine normalization findings (C15-C16, C96-C97, C136-C141). Both evaluations find these claims well-supported. OpenEval highlights specificity of effects and appropriate statistical methods, while peer reviewers explicitly confirm TRF 'normalized plasma cytokine levels' with 'reduced systemic levels of inflammatory markers.'

Perfect agreement on correlations between inflammation, sleep, and behavior (C98-C101, C142-C147). Both evaluations support these correlational findings. OpenEval notes correlation does not establish causation, while peer reviewers accept the mechanistic framework linking sleep quality to reduced inflammation and enhanced capacities.

Key difference in evaluation. OpenEval rates mechanistic inferences about cytokine causality as UNCERTAIN (C17, C102, C104, C148), noting correlational data require further experimental validation. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, explicitly endorsing the mechanistic framework that 'modifying eating patterns might improve sleep quality, leading to reduced inflammation.'

Agreement on integrative interpretation (C18, C105). Both evaluations support the view that circadian disruption contributes to symptoms. OpenEval notes causal relationships require further elucidation, while peer reviewers describe interpretation as 'supported by the provided data' and providing 'thorough understanding.'

Subtle difference in evaluation. OpenEval rates translational claims as UNCERTAIN (C19, C89-C90, C93-C94, C106-C111), noting translation requires additional validation and optimal timing is speculative. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, fully endorsing therapeutic potential and framing study around translational hypothesis for children with NDD.

OpenEval evaluated background/context claims about FXS (C1-C2, C20-C30) as SUPPORTED but noted these are established knowledge, not novel findings. Peer reviewers did not separately evaluate background claims.
OpenEval evaluated literature review claims (C31-C37) as SUPPORTED background establishing study rationale. Peer reviewers did not separately evaluate these literature summary claims.
OpenEval evaluated background claim about cytokines in FXS (C95) as SUPPORTED by appropriate citations. Peer reviewers did not separately evaluate this background claim.

OpenEval evaluated methodological validation claims (C112-C118) as SUPPORTED, noting importance of sleep measurement validation and TRF adaptation confirmation. Peer reviewers did not separately evaluate these methodological details.

Peer reviewers evaluated the observation about dissociation from general sensory hypersensitivity (C67) as SUPPORTED, treating it as valid observation about specificity. OpenEval included C67 in R6 with other anatomical findings, also rating as SUPPORTED.
